extracted.intended_audience: editors, journalists and media/legal professionals at Australian news organisations
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the Australian Press Council to determine whether an editorial (and other published material) breaches principles on accuracy, fairness, right of reply and harm (offence/distress), especially where individuals are named or implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure factual material is accurate and not misleading (General Principle 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to ensure factual material in news reports and elsewhere is accurate and not misleading, and is distinguishable from other material such as opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council emphasises that even in an editorial a publication remains obliged to take reasonable steps to ensure factual material is not misleading. Example: the statement “Many senior people at The Australian know well the work, the habits and the hubris of … Louise Milligan” was presented as a statement of fact (not merely opinion) and the Council found that inference unsustainable and misleading. Reasonable steps imply checking factual assertions and avoiding presentation that will be read as factual when it is not supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present factual material with reasonable fairness and balance (General Principle 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must ensure that factual material is presented with reasonable fairness and balance, and that writers’ expressions of opinion are not based on significantly inaccurate factual material or omission of key facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where an editorial expresses robust views, those opinions should not rest on materially inaccurate facts or important omissions. The Council found the editorial misleadingly and unfairly inferred undesirable traits about the complainant because of the way factual claims and named references were presented. Fairness and balance require avoiding unfair adverse inferences about identified individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a fair opportunity for reply when material refers adversely to a person (General Principle 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where material refers adversely to a person, a fair opportunity is to be given for a subsequent publication of a reply if that is reasonably necessary to address a possible breach of General Principle 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A right of reply should be offered if needed to correct or respond to potentially unfair adverse material. The Council noted the complainant did not seek a right of reply in this case and therefore found no breach of GP4, but GP4 stands as a procedural safeguard publications should provide when adverse personal references could create unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice unless in sufficient public interest (General Principle 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice, or a substantial risk to health or safety, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming a person in an editorial that imputes undesirable traits can be likely to cause substantial offence and distress; such harm may be justified only by a clear and sufficient public interest. The Council concluded naming the complainant was likely to cause substantial offence and distress without sufficient public interest justification, and therefore GP6 was breached. When asserting harmful claims, editors must weigh the public interest benefit and be prepared to substantiate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials have latitude but remain subject to the same factual and fairness obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: An editorial is the voice of a newspaper and is given significant latitude in expressing views, but it remains obliged to ensure factual material is not misleading and is presented with reasonable fairness and balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council recognises robust expression in editorials is permitted, but this latitude does not permit presenting unsupported factual assertions about individuals or institutions. Presentational choices that convert opinion into apparent fact can render an editorial unfair or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish opinion from factual material in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual material should be distinguishable from opinion so readers can tell what is asserted as fact and what is the writer’s view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council pointed out the disputed phrase was presented as a statement of fact rather than an opinion. Clear signalling (tone, phrasing, attribution) is required to avoid misleading readers into treating opinion as established fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make adverse imputations about identified individuals without sustainable basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should avoid implying that a named person possesses undesirable traits (e.g., lies, dissembling, being deceitful, lazy or of low integrity) unless the inference is supportable on the information before the publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council found it was an unavoidable conclusion from the editorial that the complainant was associated with 'bad, lazy, deceitful journalism' and that such an inference was not sustainable on the material before it. When naming individuals, writers should be careful that criticism of institutions does not unfairly individualise blame without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual reporting does not absolve misleading or unfair editorial assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that an editorial should be read in the context of separate news reporting or the subject’s social media do not necessarily excuse misleading or unfair assertions within the editorial itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publication argued references to the complainant must be read alongside separate reporting and the subject’s social media. The Council nonetheless assessed the editorial on its own presentation and found the inference about the complainant unsustainable. Editors should not rely solely on external context to justify unsupported claims within an editorial.
